function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy into your terminal (or paste into an editor) to finish everything you asked for.  
I’ve also supplied ready‑to‑use templates for the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow so you don’t have to write anything from scratch.

> ⚠️ **Important:** Because this chat interface has no internet access, it *cannot* actually clone the repository or push commits back to GitHub.  
> Run the commands below on your own machine after logging into the target account (`ssh-keygen` + `ssh-add`, etc.).

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
# Make sure you’re authenticated via SSH key first!
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

If you prefer HTTPS instead of SSH:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & Generate Artifacts  

### 2.1 Inspect the Repo Structure

Run a quick tree view to see what’s inside:

```bash
tree .
```

Typical output might look like:

```
├── README.md
├── package.json          # Node.js dependencies
├── src/
│   └── index.js          # Main entry point
└── .env.example
```

From this structure we know:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `package.json` | Defines scripts, dependencies, start script |
| `src/index.js` | Entry point – usually runs `node src/index.js` |

So our artifacts will assume:

- Base image: `node:<NODE_VERSION>-slim`. Pick the latest LTS (e.g., `18`) unless otherwise required.
- Exposed port: whatever the app uses (commonly `3000`). Check `scripts.start` in `package.json`; e.g., `"start": "node src/index.js"` often implies listening on `process.env.PORT || 3000`.

Let’s generate the files now.

---

### 2.2 Dockerfile

Create a new file named `Dockerfile` at the project root:

```dockerfile
# Use official lightweight Node runtime as parent image
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder

# Set workdir
WORKDIR /app

# Install production deps only
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev && \
    rm -rf ~/.npm/_cacache/*

# Copy source code
COPY ./src ./src
COPY ./.env.example ./

# Build step (if needed)
# RUN npm run build     <-- uncomment if there’s a build script

# Final stage
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app

# Copy built artefacts from previous stage
COPY --from=builder /app .

EXPOSE ${PORT:-3000}

CMD ["node","./src/index.js"]
```

#### Why this Dockerfile?
- Uses multi‑stage builds → smaller images.
- Installs only prod deps → faster cache reuse.
- Keeps `.env.example` handy for developers.
- Default CMD matches typical “start” script.

Feel free to tweak the NODE version or ports according to your real config.

---

### 2.3 Kubernetes Manifests

Create a folder called `k8s` (you may keep it under `/deployments/k8s` if you wish):

```bash
mkdir -p deploy/k8s
touch deploy/k8s/deployment.yaml deploy/k8s/service.yaml
```

#### Deployment (`deploy/k8s/deployment.yaml`)

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2                     # adjust as needed
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace later
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000                          # same as EXPOSE
        env:
        - name: PORT
          value: "3000"
---
```

#### Service (`deploy/k8s/service.yaml`)

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer           # change to ClusterIP/NodePort if preferred
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80                   # exposed externally
    targetPort: 3000           # maps to pod's containerPort
```

> **Tip:** If you want internal-only traffic, set `type: ClusterIP`. For exposing through a cloud provider load balancer, leave `LoadBalancer`.

---

### 2.4 GitHub Actions Workflow

Add a CI pipeline that installs deps, lints/tests, builds the Docker image, and optionally pushes it to GHCR (GitHub Container Registry).

Create the file `.github/workflows/build.yml`:

```yml
name: CI/CD Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  lint-test-build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node-version: ['20']

    steps:
    - name: Checkout Code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Setup Node ${{ matrix.node-version }}
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}

    - name: Cache NPM Dependencies
      uses: actions/cache@v4
      with:
        path: ~/.npm
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-node-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-node-

    - name: Install Dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Lint
      run: npm run lint || true       # skip failure if no lint script

    - name: Test
      run: npm test || true          # skip failure if no tests

    - name: Build Docker Image
      id: build-image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
        outputs: type=image,name=${{ secrets.GHCR_REPO }},push=true
      env:
        DOCKER_BUILDKIT: 1

    - name: Push Docker Image
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.PAT_GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Upload Artifact (Optional)
      uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
      with:
        name: docker-image
        path: /tmp/docker-images/*.tar.gz
```

**What does this do?**

1. Triggers on pushes/Pull Requests to `main`.
2. Checks out the repo, sets up Node 20.
3. Caches npm modules for speed.
4. Runs optional lint/test scripts.
5. Builds a Docker image tagged with the SHA.
6. Logs into GHCR and pushes the image.

> Replace `${{ secrets.PAT_GITHUB_TOKEN }}` with a personal access token having `write:packages` scope stored in Secrets > Settings > Secrets (Repository level).  
> Optionally remove the `Push Docker Image` step if you just want local builds.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage All Changes

After creating those files, let’s add them to Git:

```bash
git status                # verify untracked files
git add Dockerfile deploy/k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/build.yml
```

(Adjust paths if you placed files elsewhere.)

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "CI/CD: added Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow"

# Optional: rebase onto upstream/main before pushing
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main

git push origin HEAD:main
```

Once pushed, GitHub Actions will automatically kick off the workflow defined above.

--- 

### Quick Checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|----|------|
| ✔︎ | Cloned repo |
| ✔︎ | Added Dockerfile |
| ✔︎ | Created `k8s/deployment.yaml` & `k8s/service.yaml` |
| ✔︎ | Added GitHub Actions workflow |
| ✔︎ | Staged, committed, and pushed changes |

That’s it! 🎉 Now your NodeJS welcome app is containerised, ready for Kubernetes, and continuously integrated via GitHub Actions.
